Risk fundamentals
In the asset-threat-vulnerability model, when does risk exist?
When a threat can exploit a vulnerability in a valuable asset
Whenever an organisation owns any computer at all
Only after an attacker has been identified by name
Only when a vulnerability has a public exploit
Risk needs all three: something of value, a weakness and something that can exploit it.
m
Risk fundamentals
How is risk usually expressed in a simple risk matrix?
Likelihood multiplied by impact
Number of assets divided by staff
Patch count multiplied by servers
Firewall rules divided by alerts
A 5x5 matrix scores likelihood and impact from 1 to 5 and multiplies them.
d
Inherent and residual risk
What is the difference between inherent and residual risk?
Inherent risk is before controls; residual risk remains after controls
Inherent risk applies to hardware; residual risk applies to software
Inherent risk is accepted; residual risk must always be eliminated
Inherent risk is measured monthly; residual risk only yearly
Controls reduce inherent risk to residual risk, which leadership must judge acceptable or not.
m
Vulnerability management
Why is vulnerability management described as a lifecycle rather than a project?
New vulnerabilities and assets appear continuously
It must be completed once before an audit
It ends after the first full network scan
It only runs when a breach has occurred
Discovery, prioritisation, remediation and verification repeat continuously.
m
CVE
What is a CVE identifier?
A public reference number for a specific known vulnerability
A severity score from 0 to 10 for a vulnerability
A patch released by the software vendor
A certificate showing a system is secure
CVE names vulnerabilities; CVSS scores their severity.
m
CVSS
What does a CVSS base score measure?
The technical severity of a vulnerability
The business value of the affected asset
The number of attackers exploiting it
The cost of applying the patch
The base score reflects exploitability and impact characteristics, not organisational context.
d
CVSS
Which CVSS v3.1 base score range is rated Critical?
Critical is 9.0-10.0, High 7.0-8.9, Medium 4.0-6.9 and Low 0.1-3.9.
d
Prioritisation
A CVSS 9.8 flaw affects an isolated lab system, and a CVSS 7.5 flaw affects an internet-facing payment server under active exploitation. Which should be fixed first?
The payment server flaw, because exposure and active exploitation raise its risk
The lab flaw, because a higher CVSS score always means higher priority
Neither, because scores below 10 do not need urgent action
Both at once, because CVSS scores cannot be compared
Prioritisation combines severity with business context, exposure and threat activity.
d
CVSS vectors
In a CVSS vector, what does AV:N indicate?
The vulnerability can be exploited over the network
The vulnerability needs no authentication at all
The vulnerability affects only availability
The vulnerability has no known exploit
Attack Vector: Network means remote exploitation is possible, which typically raises severity.
m
Risk register
What is a risk register?
A record of identified risks with scores, owners and treatment plans
A list of every employee's login history
A database of malware signatures for antivirus
A firewall rule set exported to a spreadsheet
The register tracks each risk from identification to treatment and review.
d
Risk register
Why does each risk in a register need a named owner?
Someone must be accountable for its treatment and review
Owners pay for any losses the risk causes personally
Auditors only read risks that have owners' signatures
Unowned risks are removed from the register automatically
Accountability ensures treatment actions happen and risks are reviewed on schedule.
m
Risk frameworks
Which framework is used to certify an information security management system?
ISO/IEC 27001
NIST SP 800-61
MITRE ATT&CK
CVSS v3.1
Organisations can be certified against ISO/IEC 27001; the others are guidance or scoring systems.
d
FAIR
What does the FAIR model add to risk analysis?
Quantification of risk in financial terms
A list of controls required by law
A scoring system for individual CVEs
A taxonomy of malware families
FAIR estimates loss event frequency and magnitude to express risk in money.
d
NIST RMF
What is the NIST Risk Management Framework primarily used for?
A lifecycle for selecting, implementing and monitoring controls on systems
A database of attacker techniques and tools
A scale for calibrating likelihood ratings
A certification scheme for security professionals
RMF steps include categorise, select, implement, assess, authorise and monitor.
m
Calibration
Why should likelihood and impact scales be defined with concrete ranges?
So different people give consistent ratings
So that every risk is rated as High
So that impact can be ignored in reports
So that only experts can read the scores
Undefined labels like 'Medium' mean different things to different people.
d
Calibration
On a likelihood scale where 'Likely' means 1 to 12 events per year, how often might such an event occur?
Between about once a year and monthly
Between weekly and daily
Less than once every ten years
More than once every hour
One to twelve events a year ranges from yearly to monthly.
d
Calibration
What is a common mistake when estimating impact?
Confusing the loss from one event with the annual loss
Using money instead of colours to describe impact
Including safety effects in critical systems
Basing likelihood on threat intelligence data
Impact per event and annualised loss are different numbers; mixing them distorts scores.
d
Bias
Why do teams use reference data and calibration exercises when estimating risk?
To reduce overconfidence and other cognitive biases
To make risk scores higher for budget requests
To avoid involving business owners in decisions
To remove the need for any risk register
Calibration training and data improve the accuracy of expert estimates.
m
Qualitative analysis
What is a strength of qualitative risk analysis?
It is quick and easy to communicate
It always produces precise money values
It needs extensive historical loss data
It removes all subjectivity from ratings
Qualitative ratings are fast but subjective; quantitative methods need more data.
d
Quantitative analysis
An asset worth 2,000,000 has an exposure factor of 0.25 and an annual rate of occurrence of 0.1. What is the annualised loss expectancy?
d
Quantitative analysis
If a control costs 80,000 a year and reduces ALE from 60,000 to 10,000, is it cost-justified on these figures alone?
No, because it costs more than the 50,000 reduction it buys
Yes, because any reduction in ALE justifies the cost
Yes, because ALE falls below the control's cost
No, because ALE can never be reduced by controls
The control's value is the ALE reduction (50,000), which is less than its annual cost (80,000).
m
Qualitative failure
What does it suggest when every risk in a register is rated High?
The scales are not calibrated and cannot guide priorities
The organisation has an excellent security programme
Risk analysis has been completed correctly
No further controls are needed anywhere
If everything is High, nothing is prioritised; calibration fixes this.
m
Risk treatment
Which are the four common risk treatment options?
Mitigate, transfer, avoid and accept
Detect, delete, deny and defer
Patch, scan, log and alert
Encrypt, hash, sign and verify
Treatment reduces, shares, removes or knowingly accepts risk.
m
Risk transfer
Buying cyber insurance is an example of which treatment?
Transfer
Avoidance
Mitigation
Acceptance
Insurance shifts some financial impact to another party, but not the responsibility to protect data.
d
Risk avoidance
A company stops offering a risky legacy service rather than securing it. Which treatment is this?
Avoidance
Transfer
Acceptance
Mitigation
Removing the activity removes the risk.
d
Risk acceptance
What must accompany a formal risk acceptance?
A documented decision by an authorised owner, with a review date
Deletion of the risk from the register
A promise from IT that the risk will never occur
Approval from every employee in the company
Acceptance is a managed decision, not neglect, and is revisited when conditions change.
d
Remediation SLAs
Why do organisations set remediation SLAs by severity, such as 15 days for critical findings?
To make sure the most serious issues are fixed fastest and tracked
To guarantee attackers wait until the SLA ends
To allow low-severity findings to be ignored forever
To meet a legal rule that applies in every country
SLAs turn prioritisation into measurable commitments; exceptions need formal approval.
m
Continuous risk management
Why is an annual risk assessment alone not enough?
Threats, assets and vulnerabilities change throughout the year
Auditors require assessments every week
Risk scores expire after thirty days
Annual assessments are prohibited by ISO 27001
Continuous monitoring keeps the register current as the environment changes.
d
Exceptions
A server cannot be patched because a vendor no longer supports it. What is the right handling?
Record an exception with compensating controls and a review date
Remove the server from the asset inventory
Rate its risk as Low so it leaves the report
Disable logging on it to avoid alerts
Compensating controls such as isolation reduce risk while the exception is tracked.
m
Communication
How should a risk be described to business leaders?
In terms of business impact and likelihood
Only as a list of CVE numbers
Only in technical port and protocol terms
Without any recommendation or owner
Leaders decide on business terms; technical detail belongs in supporting material.
